# Leveraging antibiotic hormesis for cryptic natural product discovery

**Authors:** Joon Soo An; Ellysia N Overton; Mohammad R Seyedsayamdost

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 | bDepartment of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544

## Abstract

Microbial natural products are a foundational source of therapeutic agents, yet a vast majority remain inaccessible due to the limited expression of their biosynthetic gene clusters under standard laboratory conditions. To address this challenge, we developed a simple and broadly applicable screening approach based on the idea of antibiotic hormesis wherein high-dose growth-inhibitory antibiotics serve as low-dose elicitors of secondary metabolites. We generated an in-house library of all available clinical antibiotics and exposed nine phylogenetically diverse bacteria to high-dose growth inhibition and low-dose metabolite stimulation assays. The approach revealed the induction of cryptic metabolites with every strain tested. Four of these were selected for scale-up fermentation and comprehensive metabolomic analysis, leading to the identification of eight known but strain-novel cryptic metabolites and nine structurally unique, previously undescribed natural products. These findings underscore the utility of the antibiotic hormesis approach as a rapid and scalable platform for the discovery of natural products and therapeutic leads. Moreover, the consistent elicitation of cryptic metabolites highlights the generalizability of low-dose antibiotics as key signaling molecules in microbial metabolic regulation. Beyond expanding the repertoire of accessible natural products, this work lays the foundation for systematic studies into the molecular and ecological mechanisms that govern cryptic metabolite biosynthesis.

Keywords: natural products, cryptic metabolites, low-dose antibiotics, bacteria

Natural products have been a cornerstone of therapeutic discovery (1). Over the past century, compounds such as penicillin, lovastatin, and semaglutide have revolutionized the treatment of infectious diseases, cardiovascular disorders, and metabolic syndromes, respectively. These and other natural product remedies, especially antibiotics and anticancer agents, exemplify the profound therapeutic potential embedded in microbial genomes. However, despite decades of intensive natural product research, recent genome sequencing efforts show that we have only scratched the surface of microbial chemical diversity. The majority of natural product biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are sparingly expressed or transcriptionally silent, also referred to as cryptic, under standard laboratory growth conditions (2–4). As a result, their products have gone undetected in conventional drug discovery campaigns. New methodologies are needed to access and leverage this hidden repertoire of structurally and functionally diverse natural products (5–11).

Several strategies have recently emerged with the goal of stimulating the production of cryptic metabolites. Among these, we have contributed high-throughput elicitor screening (HiTES), a forward chemical genetics approach that systematically screens small molecules for their ability to induce the expression of silent BGCs (7). HiTES has broad applicability as it avoids elaborate cloning or genetic manipulation procedures and directly links chemical elicitors to metabolic outputs. A striking and recurrent finding from HiTES has been the identification of low-dose antibiotics as the most effective inducers of silent BGCs (7, 12–17). Across diverse microbial taxa, including soil-dwelling actinomycetes, marine bacteria, human microbiome strains, (18) and fungi, (19) subinhibitory concentrations of antibiotics have repeatedly been identified as inducers of silent BGCs, leading to the production of otherwise undetected metabolites. The underlying mechanism of this antibiotic hormesis effect has been investigated in a few cases, revealing that low-dose antibiotics act on their canonical cellular targets, similar to their high-dose, lethal counterparts. However, rather than triggering cell death, these sublethal perturbations activate stress response pathways that include the induction of otherwise dormant secondary metabolite BGCs, in some cases, via canonical transcriptional regulators (17, 20–24).

These observations have led us to formulate a simple yet powerful hypothesis that forms the motivation for the current work: We pose that antibiotics, which inhibit growth at high doses, can broadly act as inducers of cryptic metabolism at low doses. If true, this would offer an exceptionally straightforward approach to cryptic metabolite discovery, one that requires no cloning, genetic engineering, nor elaborate chemical screens. Instead, it would rely on standard antibiotic assays to first identify “high-dose killers,” followed by testing those same antibiotics at subinhibitory concentrations in conjunction with HPLC-MS-based metabolomics to identify “low-dose elicitors” of cryptic metabolites (Fig. 1). This approach would leverage antibiotic hormesis in the search for novel natural products and obviate the need for high-throughput screens, instead relying on simple phenotypic screens and subsequent metabolic profiling with a small number of antibiotics.

In this study, we systematically test the antibiotic hormesis idea across nine well-studied phylogenetically and ecologically diverse bacterial strains. Our results revealed cryptic metabolites in every single screen. Not every high-dose growth-inhibitor served as a low-dose inducer of secondary metabolism, but we find that >40% of antibiotics exhibit this phenotype among the strains tested, resulting in clear metabolomic shifts. We scaled up cultures of four representative strains under eliciting conditions, performed metabolomic profiling and compound isolation, and identified a eight new-to-strain natural products as well as nine novel cryptic metabolites, including a structurally distinct class that we term beddingiolide. These findings reinforce the emerging view that antibiotics do not merely function as antimicrobial agents at high doses but also as potent modulators of microbial gene expression and secondary metabolism at low doses. They further demonstrate that the antibiotic hormesis strategy is not only conceptually sound but also highly effective in practice, offering a rapid and simple approach for natural product discovery. Antibiotic hormesis thus provides a new approach for accessing the hidden biosynthetic potential of microbes as well as enriching the chemical and functional space of secondary metabolites and possible drug leads.

## Results

Creation of an in-house antibiotic library and hormesis screens. To assess the antibiotics hormesis idea, we first created a custom library of clinical antibiotics. While our prior libraries contained a small number of antibiotics, which were often identified as elicitors, we designed the current library to consist exclusively of antibiotics. Approximately 180 antibiotics have been approved by the FDA. Of these, we were able to procure 133, which were dissolved in DMSO or water at a stock concentration of 1 mM (SI Appendix, Table S1), with the goal of screening these at high doses (~20 μM); those that inhibit growth would then be tested at low doses (1 to 5 μM) using UPLC-qTOF-MS as a read-out for metabolite production.

We selected nine representative bacterial strains across numerous genera, including Gram-positive (Streptomyces, Amycolatopsis, and Bacillus) and Gram-negative bacteria (Burkholderia, Xenorhabdus, Phaeobacter, and Serratia). Most strains have previously been heavily mined for secondary metabolites; these were chosen to provide a rigorous test for the antibiotics hormesis approach. We conducted growth inhibition assays for each strain, wherein end point growth was plotted relative to a vehicle-treated control at high doses of the antibiotic library (Fig. 2). With Gram-negatives, Bacillus, and Amycolatopsis, we used optical density at 600 nm (OD600) to monitor growth, whereas the resazurin assay was used as a read-out with streptomycetes. Hits were defined as those antibiotics that reduced growth to 40% or less relative to the vehicle control. The screen identified 400 hits across the nine strains. These are tabulated for each strain along with the percent growth observed (SI Appendix, Table S2). For example, minocycline, spiramycin, and cefditoren were efficient high-dose killers with the actinomycetes, whereas thiamphenicol, rifabutin, and rifampicin appeared frequently with the Gram-negatives.

To prioritize these, we selected 10 antibiotics per strain that exhibited the highest levels of growth inhibition and screened them against the corresponding strain at low-doses in the 1 to 5 μM range. Of the 90 antibiotics tested in this manner across nine diverse strains, we found 43% of high-dose growth inhibitors to induce a metabolic response at low doses, as determined by UPLC-qTOF-MS (Fig. 3). Overall, we noted distinct differential profiles with these antibiotics and recorded nearly a dozen previously unidentified metabolites per strain, highlighting the efficiency of this approach for triggering production of cryptic metabolites (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2). We were able to rapidly dereplicate several known cryptic metabolites using the Dictionary of Natural Products (CHEMnetBASE); most of these are new to the strains we examined but previously characterized from other bacteria. For example, Amycolatopsis decaplanensis produced significant levels of octacosamicin A in response to low-dose minocycline (Fig. 3A and SI Appendix, Fig. S1) (25). Xenorhabdus beddingii was found to synthesize rhabdopeptide K in response to thiamphenicol (Fig. 3B) (26). Streptomyces canus produced octalactin B and canucin A in response to cefditoren and spiramycin, respectively (Fig. 3 C and D) (27, 28). Streptomyces parvus overproduced actinomycin D in the presence of low-dose methacycline (Fig. 3E) (29). Finally, we found prodigiosin and serramatolides in response to rifabutin in cultures of Serratia marcescens (Fig. 3 F–I) (30, 31). BGCs for each of these could be identified as well. More importantly, we identified several novel metabolites from Burkholderia pyrrocinia, X. beddingii, S. canus, and A. decaplanensis, and these compounds were next investigated further (Fig. 4 and SI Appendix, Fig. S2).

Low-dose rifampicin triggers production of cryptic metabolites in B. pyrrocinia. Rifampicin was lethal to B. pyrrocinia at 20 μM. Low-dose rifampicin (1 μM), however, triggered production of several cryptic metabolites in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 4 A–C). We purified three compounds from large-scale cultures in the presence of low-dose rifampicin and solved their structures using one-dimensional (1D)/two-dimensional (2D) NMR spectral analysis as well as high-resolution mass spectrometry (HR-MS). The most abundant of these, which we named pyrrocinamide A, purified as an amorphous solid with a deduced molecular formula of C20H42N2O2 and one degree of unsaturation (SI Appendix, Table S3). We observed one sp3 methyl group (δH 0.85; δC 14.4), 17 sp3 methylenes (δH 1.20 to 3.04; δC 22.6 to 37.4), one oxygenated methine group (δH 3.57; δC 68.0), and one amide-proton (δH 7.86) as a part of two spin systems (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 and Table S4). One of these consisted of an N-acylated 3-hydroxycadaverine substructure and the other of a straight-chain C16 acyl group. Two key HMBC correlations from the 1′-NH (7.86 ppm) and the C-2-H2 (35.8 ppm) to the C-1-carbonyl carbon (δC 172.8) indicated that the two spin systems are connected by an amide bond, thus accounting for the degree of unsaturation in pyrrocinamide A and completing its planar structure (Fig. 5A). Assignment of absolute configuration at C-2′ was first attempted with the phenylglycine methyl ester (PGME) method. However, the derivatized products were undetectable via HPLC–MS. As a result, we resorted to electronic circular dichroism (ECD) calculations (32). The experimental ECD spectrum of pyrrocinamide A showed a negative cotton effect at −220 nm (Fig. 5B). The calculated spectrum of the 2′- S diastereomer was close to the experimental ECD spectrum, indicating that C-2′ is S-configured.

Two additional compounds, pyrrocinamides B and C, were characterized with similar features (Fig. 5C). Both contained the N-acylated 3-hydroxycadaverine substructure but incorporated an olefin in the C16 (variant B) or C18 (variant C) acyl group, as evidenced by overlapping methine carbons (δC 130.2, SI Appendix, Figs. S4 and S5 and Tables S5 and S6). The position and geometry of the double bonds was marred by overlapping proton signals (δH ~5.34). To assign this feature, olefin cross-metathesis and subsequent HPLC–MS analysis were applied, ultimately demonstrating that it resides between C-11 and C-12 (Materials and Methods and SI Appendix, Fig. S6) (33). The configurations of the double bonds were established using 13C chemical shifts. It has been reported that aliphatic carbons adjacent to a Z-olefins in a long hydrocarbon chain resonate at δC 28 to 30 ppm, while those near an E-double bond resonate at δC 42 to 43 ppm allowing for a clear distinction between E/Z configurations (34). Since the chemical shifts of C-10 and C-13 were observed at δC 27.1 in pyrrocinamide B and δC 28.3 in pyrrocinamide C, the double bond in both variants was deduced to be Z-configured, thus completing the structure of the pyrrocinamides, new cryptic metabolites elicited using antibiotics hormesis (Fig. 5C).

Low-dose trimethoprim and beddingiolide production in X. beddingii. We likewise followed up on another cryptic metabolite elicited by low-dose trimethoprim in X. beddingii. Trimethoprim has been observed as a low-dose elicitor before and its mechanism of action has been addressed in Burkholderia thailandensis, where it triggered production of the cytotoxin malleicyprol/malleilactone (14). In X. beddingii, low-dose trimethoprim triggered production of a compound with a molecular formula, derived from HR-MS, of C24H42N2O6S with five degrees of unsaturation (Fig. 4D, SI Appendix, Table S3). This compound, which we termed beddingiolide, was not at all produced under standard growth conditions. Comprehensive analysis of 1D/2D NMR data revealed three carbonyl carbons (δC 173.1, 172.9, and 170.7), two olefinic carbons (δC 148.4 and 133.7), three oxygenated carbons (δC 80.0, 74.9, and 68.0), 12 aliphatic carbons (δC 39.1 to 24.5), one fully substituted carbon (δH 39.1), three methyl groups (δC 21.0, 20.3, and 14.0), two amide protons (δH 8.04 and 7.68), and two alcohols (δH 5.50 and 4.55) (Fig. 6A and SI Appendix, Fig. S7 and Table S7). Four out of the five degrees of unsaturation were explained by the existence of three carbonyl carbons and one double bond, suggesting that beddingiolide has a ring moiety.

(B) Configurational assignment at C-4 and C-12 using experimental ECD spectra and comparison to calculated ECD spectra for the four diastereomers indicated. (C) Final structure of beddingiolide.*

Detailed analysis of a COSY NMR spectrum revealed six spin systems. Five of these were linked by HMBC correlations, revealing a pantetheine-like moiety, containing an alkylated thiol and an α, γ-dihydroxy-β, β-dimethyl acyl group. The other major spin system consisted of an octyl group. HMBC correlations, notably from H2–1′ (δH 2.18) and H-4 (δH 5.22), showed that these are linked through an α, β-unsaturated γ-lactone, thus establishing the planar structure of beddingiolide (Fig. 6A). In order to assign the absolute configurations of the two stereogenic centers, C-4 and C-12, ECD calculations were used. The CD spectrum of the isolated natural product matched the calculated (4R, 12R)-diastereomer, thus completing the structure of this unusual, substituted, and unsaturated γ-lactone (Fig. 6 B and C).

Xenoptides, cryptic cyclic depsipeptides induced by thiamphenicol. Beddingiolide was not the only cryptic metabolite produced by X. beddingii. Aside from trimethoprim, thiamphenicol also exhibited a high-dose killing and low-dose stimulating phenotype. Specifically, we observed induction of two large compounds with [M+H]+ of 1401.8738 and 1399.8618, molecules that had no matches in natural product databases and which we have termed xenoptides A and B, respectively. Isolation from large-scale cultures in the presence of thiamphenicol and extensive NMR and chemical analysis allowed us to solve the structures of these new peptides (SI Appendix, Figs. S8–S10). Comprehensive analysis of 1D/2D NMR data revealed the presence of two prolines, two threonines, four valines, two isoleucines, and one each of leucine, alanine, glycine, and the noncanonical amino acid, β-alanine. COSY/TOCSY correlations between H3–4′ (δH 0.86), H2–3′ (δH 1.46), and H2-2′ (δH 2.26 and 2.21), along with the HMBC correlations from H2-2′ to C-1′ (δC 171.7) assigned a butanoic acid moiety (N-Bu) (SI Appendix, Fig. S8 and Table S8). The 15 identified carbonyl groups and two prolines accounted for 17 out of 18 degrees of unsaturation, suggesting xenoptide A is a cyclic peptide. ROESY correlations between H2-2′ and H2-5 (δH 3.50 and 3.38) confirmed that the N-Bu moiety is linked at the N-terminus at Pro-1. Due to the presence of multiple aliphatic amino acids, such as Gly, Ala, Ile, Leu, and Val, the connectivity between amino acids was challenging to establish through HMBC and ROESY NMR spectral data alone, except for the linkages of N-Bu-Pro–Thr–Gly–Val–Val and Ala–β-Ala–Pro.

We resorted to detailed HR-MS/MS analysis of both the intact peptide and the base-catalyzed hydrolysate product, revealing the sequences of N-Bu-Pro–Thr–Gly–Val–Val–Ile/Leu and N-Bu-Pro–Thr–Gly–Val–Val–Ile/Leu–Thr–Val–Ile/Leu– Ile/Leu–Ala–β-Ala–Pro–Val, thus suggesting an ester linkage between Thr-2 and Val-4 (SI Appendix, Tables S9 and S10 and Figs. S11 and S12). We supplemented the data with xenoptide isolated in the presence of Ile-d10 or Leu-d10 to clarify the identities of these residues (SI Appendix, Figs. S13 and S14). We found Ile incorporation into the linear portion of the intact peptide and both Ile and Leu insertion into the hydrolysate, which ultimately led to the proposed structure shown for xenoptide A (Fig. 7).

Xenoptide B, a second analog, was analyzed in a similar manner, with the 1D NMR spectrum exhibiting a high similarity to that of variant A (SI Appendix, Fig. S9 and Table S11). Comprehensive analysis of its spectral properties showed that xenoptide B carries an additional double bond conjugated to a carbonyl group in the N-terminal acyl group, allowing us to identify it as trans-crotonic acid, thus completing the planar structures of the new cryptic cyclic depsipeptides (Fig. 7).

Advanced Marfey’s analysis showed the presence of both d/l-Thr and d/l -Val. To assign the absolute configurations of α-carbons in xenoptides, we sought to identify the xenoptide BGC. Initially, we analyzed the draft genome sequence of X. beddingii DSM 4764 using antiSMASH (version 7.0) (35). However, we could not locate a nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) BGC that contained 14 modules. The draft genome consisted of a number of contigs, suggesting that perhaps the whole BGC sequence had not been captured. We, therefore, resequenced the genome of X. beddingii DSM 4764 yielding a 3.87 Mb chromosome that revealed a large NRPS operon along with 14 other natural product BGCs, demonstrating a significant potential for secondary metabolite biosynthesis (SI Appendix, Table S12). The large NRPS BGC (SI Appendix, Table S13), ~65 kb in size, consists of three modular NRPSs (xnp C–E) that encode 14 modules with adenylation (A)-domain specificities (36) that matched the sequence inferred from HR-MS/ MS analysis: Pro-1–Thr-1–Gly–Val-1–Val-2–Ile-1–Thr-2–Val-3– Ile-2–Leu–Ala–β-Ala–Pro-2–Val-4. The A-domain specific to β-Ala was confirmed by manual inspection of the selectivity-conferring residues and comparison with the xenoamicins (37), a structurally related cyclic depsipeptide that also carries β-Ala (SI Appendix, Fig. S14). Further analysis suggested the presence of dual condensation/epimerization (C/E) domains in modules 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12, thus indicating that Thr-1, Val-2, Thr-2, Ile-2, and Ala are all d-configured (SI Appendix, Fig. S15) (38). These findings complete the structural assignment of the xenoptides and suggest a plausible biosynthetic pathway (Fig. 7).

Biological evaluation of novel cryptic metabolites. We explored any antimicrobial and antifungal activities of pyrrocinamides, beddingiolide, and xenoptides by conducting dose–response assays with Escherichia coli K12, Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1, S. marcescens NRRL B-2544, Bacillus subtilis 168, Enterococcus faecalis OG1RF, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae Y00000 (SI Appendix, Tables S14–S16). However, no inhibitory activity was observed against these strains under our assay conditions. The functions of these molecules remain to be determined; their production and isolation facilitate these future functional studies.

Additional cryptic metabolites. Finally, we identified several analogs of previously known natural products, which were characterized by HR-MS/MS-based dereplication and NMR spectroscopy (Fig. 4 G–J). We identified aspartocins F and G, two new analogs of a previously known class of acylated cyclic peptides with several non-canonical residues. These were induced by low-dose spiramycin in S. canus. We also identified octacosamicin C, a variant of the known compound from A. decaplanensis. This long, linear polyketide was identified from A. decaplanensis in response to low-dose minocycline (Fig. 4 I and J), adding three additional compounds to the group of nine new metabolites identified via antibiotic hormesis. These results also provide additional elicitor/cryptic metabolite pairs, which will enable detailed elicitor structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies in the future and allow us to examine why certain classes of antibiotics give rise to specific cryptic metabolites.

## Conclusions

Our prior studies showed that low-dose antibiotics are the most effective elicitors across numerous bacterial genera (7, 12–17). With several antibiotics, we examined the mechanism of induction and found them to act through the same target at low and high doses and use canonical stress response-related transcriptional regulators (13, 14). These observations set up a simple hypothesis that we have tested in the current study: High-dose growth-inhibitors can act as low-dose inducers of secondary metabolism. If true, it would provide for a remarkably simple approach for activating cryptic natural products with routine methods that have now been used for decades. This approach would consist of finding high-dose growth inhibitors using simple bioassays and screening these at low, subinhibitory doses to monitor cryptic metabolite production using facile read-outs, such as HPLC-MS. It would obviate any need for screening random culture variations such as in OSMAC (39), extensive cloning of gene clusters often conducted in heterologous expression or synthetic biology approaches, bacterial genetics in forward and reverse genetics approaches, or high-throughput small molecule screens in forward chemical genetics approaches (9).

Our results show that this antibiotic hormesis approach is highly effective and that screening a small number of high-dose growth inhibitors can yield low-dose elicitors. While we screened a library of 133 antibiotics, our results show that statistically a much smaller number will be sufficient: given that 43% of high-dose growth inhibitors acted as low-dose elicitors, the number of antibiotics can be significantly reduced to simplify the approach even further. The antibiotic hormesis method is thus the simplest yet among a cadre of approaches that have been developed in recent years to access natural products from sparingly expressed or transcriptionally silent BGCs.

The concentration-dependent effects of antibiotics have been known for some time, with low doses often eliciting profound, nonlethal physiological responses (4, 12, 40–44). Sublethal concentrations can trigger global transcriptional reprogramming, modulate quorum sensing, and alter biofilm dynamics. The ability of low-dose antibiotics to activate otherwise silent BGCs has emerged as a compelling extension of this concept and aside from using them to access cryptic metabolites, as we show in the current work, the insights into the low-dose regime suggest that antibiotics can function as cues that, through alteration of bacterial secondary metabolism, can reshape polymicrobial communities and microbiomes in diverse settings.

Future directions for this work are at least threefold. First, the biological activities of the newly identified cryptic metabolites remain to be fully established. In our initial antimicrobial and antifungal assays against the selected panel of strains, no inhibitory activities were observed under the conditions tested. Nevertheless, given their structural novelty, it is plausible that these molecules could exhibit interesting bioactivities. As many secondary metabolites are produced in response to competitive pressures in natural environments, their biological targets may span beyond bacteria, potentially including other eukaryotic strains or symbiotic hosts. Second, a key unanswered question is how sublethal antibiotics trigger the activation of silent BGCs. We have explored this question with trimethoprim and piperacillin (13, 14), but it needs to be examined more broadly and comprehensively to perhaps identify key governing principles or commonalities in this process. One intriguing hypothesis, borne out of studies with lethal doses, is that oxidative stress could be a common factor (13). We have observed oxidative stress with several antibiotics, including piperacillin, cephalosporins, and phenylpropanoids, but it remains to be seen if it underpins induction by low-dose antibiotics more broadly (13, 45). Understanding the molecular basis of this elicitation, including any underlying elicitor SAR, will be crucial for gaining fundamental insights into the ecological roles of secondary metabolites and the triggers that govern their production. Finally, the antibiotic hormesis approach can now be used systematically with any culturable microbial host in the search for yet new, cryptic natural products.

## Supplementary Material

Microbial natural products are a rich source of therapeutic agents, yet many remain undiscovered due to the transcriptionally silent nature of their biosynthetic genes under standard laboratory conditions. Here, we present a simple and effective method to unlock this cryptic metabolome using a basic screening approach that relies on antibiotic hormesis, wherein high-dose growth-inhibitors are leveraged as low-dose stimulators of secondary metabolism. This is the simplest method yet for identifying cryptic metabolites as it avoids genetic procedures, molecular biology, or high-throughput screens. By facilitating access to previously hidden metabolites, this strategy opens avenues for natural product discovery and therapeutic lead identification. Beyond its practical utility, our findings motivate investigations into the mechanisms by which low-dose antibiotics affect microbial metabolism.

## ABSTRACT

Biofilm-forming bacteria have the potential to contribute to the health, physiology, behavior and ecology of the host and serve as its first line of defense against adverse conditions in the environment. While metabarcoding and metagenomic information furthers our understanding of microbiome composition, fewer studies use cultured samples to study the diverse interactions among the host and its microbiome, as cultured representatives are often lacking. This study examines the surface microbiomes cultured from three shallow-water coral species and two whale species. These unique marine animals place strong selective pressures on their microbial symbionts and contain members under similar environmental and anthropogenic stress. We developed an intense cultivation procedure, utilizing a suite of culture conditions targeting a rich assortment of biofilm-forming microorganisms. We identified 592 microbial isolates contained within 15 bacterial orders representing 50 bacterial genera, and two fungal species. Culturable bacteria from coral and whale samples paralleled taxonomic groups identified in culture-independent surveys, including 29% of all bacterial genera identified in the Megaptera novaeangliae skin microbiome through culture-independent methods. This microbial repository provides raw material and biological input for more nuanced studies which can explore how members of the microbiome both shape their micro-niche and impact host fitness.

Keywords: bacteria; SSU rRNA; coral; whale; microbiome; skin

## INTRODUCTION

The epidermis is an animal’s first line of defense against the external environment, yet not impervious to environmental influences. The dermis of an organism can be thought of as its own ecosystem, hosting a diverse microbial milieu, where the composition of communities is driven by both endogenous host factors and the exogenous environment. In marine ecosystems, surface-associated microbes must contend with unpredictable external variables including temperature, pH, salinity fluctuations and skin/mucus shedding by the host. The animal surface microbiome plays a significant role in the health of the host by protecting the body against transient pathogenic microorganisms, selecting for antibiotic-producing commensal strains, playing critical roles in host nutrition and significantly impacting immune system development (Nelson et al. 2015; Bourne, Morrow and Webster 2016; Apprill 2017; Ross, Rodrigues Hoffmann and Neufeld 2019). Often marine animal surfaces are referred to as ‘hot spots’ of microbial diversity. These environments are dominated by unique assemblages of host-specific bacteria capable of generating specific microenvironments that promote higher-level microbial community organization, including the production of shielding biofilm matrices, antiprotozoal factors and chemical compounds that assist in protection from predators, viruses and environmental stressors (Bik et al. 2016; Dang and Lovell 2016). The uniqueness of surface-associated microbiota in both their genetic composition and functional roles in comparison to their free-living counterparts (Burke et al. 2011) indicates either an active role of the hosts in recruitment of epibiotic bacteria or a passive mechanism of colonization based on the eukaryotic surface and exudates (Wahl et al. 2012). The surface microbiomes of both cetaceans (Nelson et al. 2015) and coral (Rosenberg et al. 2007; Zaneveld et al. 2016) have been studied to elucidate the role of the microbial community on the health, persistence and resilience of these keystone and habitat-forming species. In corals, it is well known that their resident microalgal symbionts mediate host physiology. However, it has been suggested that bacteria, archaea and fungi participate in cycling of nutrients and organic matter in coral as well (Apprill 2017). While coral microbial communities are often host specific, spatially restrictive and can be highly stable across geographic and environmental conditions, oversimplification of host–microbe association via broad profiling studies can miss low abundance taxa that contribute to physiologically significant interactions with their hosts (Bourne, Morrow and Webster 2016). Similarly, marine mammals, particularly cetaceans, are considered sentinel species in marine ecosystems (Bossart 2011). There are few microbiome studies in cetaceans and still fewer that target members of the skin microbiome (Chiarello et al. 2017; Hooper et al. 2019; Apprill et al. 2020). Recent investigations into the skin microbiome of cetaceans have suggested the existence of species-specific assemblages that can change seasonally (Bierlich et al. 2017). These assemblages can also be linked to the presence of epiphytic diatoms (Hooper et al. 2019) and are shown to be distinct from surrounding planktonic samples (Chiarello et al. 2017), suggesting ecological and evolutionary forces including the unique features of an animal’s epidermis have shaped cetacean skin microbiomes. The availability of sequence data is rapidly readjusting our view of how bacterial communities associated with marine organisms vary in composition depending on host type and environment (Vega Thurber et al. 2009; Sunagawa, Woodley and

Medina 2010; Barott et al. 2011; Hentschel et al. 2012; Sison- Mangus et al. 2014; Cooper and Smith 2015; Rouco, Haley and Dyhrman 2016). However, there is a gap in microbial diversity obtained between sequencing-based techniques and culturedependent isolation of strains. This study therefore sought to identify key features of animal surfaces and marine environments in order to recapitulate environmental conditions with the goal of isolating as diverse a complement of surface microbiome representatives possible from the dermis of two species of whale (Delphinapterus leucas and Megaptera novaeangliae) and the mucus and tissue from three species of coral (Porites astreoides, Acropora palmata and Millepora alcicornis). Six culture conditions were used in this study and chosen based on either previous success in culturing marine microbes or were developed here using knowledge of features associated with the dermis surface chemistry and microbial signaling processes. A total of three media variations used marine agar (MA), combining an agar and a commercially available marine broth base, and is a widely used media type demonstrated to yield biologically diverse microbial flora because of its nutrient richness (Mincer et al. 2002). One marine agar variation contained the antimicrobial enzyme, lysozyme (LYS), which is produced by cetaceans within the upper lamellae of the stratum corneum of the dermis and may select for microbes resistant to this non-specific defense mechanism (Seegers and Meyer 2004; Mouton and Botha 2012). Another marine agar variation contained both the secondary messenger cyclic adenosine monophosphate, shown to regulate bacterial metabolism, virulence gene expression, flagella mobility, surface attachment and biofilm formation (Smith, Wolfgang and Lory 2004; Fuchs et al. 2010; Ono et al. 2014; Dang and Lovell 2016), and N-(oxo-hexanoyl)-homoserine lactone, a homoserine lactone used by the majority of Gram-negative bacteria with quorum sensing ability (HSL-AMP; Bruns, Cypionka and Overmann 2002). Acylhomoserine lactone signals are known to mediate interspecies communication, biofilm formation and community structure (Wang et al. 2020). Lower nutrient media types included Actinobacteria-selecting media (AC; Okami and Hotta 1988) and a low nutrient media (R2A) containing chitin as both an energy source and substrata, that facilitates slower-growing, oligotrophic microbes (Reasoner and Geldreich 1985). The final media type selected for marine fungi (KJ; Kjer et al. 2010). Here we demonstrate the cultivation of 592 isolates contained within 15 bacterial orders representing 50 bacterial genera and two fungal species isolated from 25 cetacean and coral samples, indicating targeted cultivation by use of media additives and intensive microbial cultivation efforts yields high microbial diversity in comparison to other published efforts. Multivariate analyses demonstrate that microbial diversity is associated with sampled species rather than media variation, although different media variations and host surfaces were successful in culturing potentially phylogenetically distinct strains based on SSU rRNA variation. With this new microbial repository from diverse animal hosts, we can now begin to explore how interactions among microbial community members can impact host fitness.

Sample collection

Skin samples were obtained from North Atlantic humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) on the Gulf of Maine feeding ground in May and June, 2016 as part of a long-term population research program led by the Center for Coastal Studies (CCS). Samples were collected from twelve free-ranging individuals as either sloughed skin or biopsy sampling techniques. Biopsy samples were collected from the dorsal flank using a crossbow equipped with a hollow biopsy dart capable of obtaining a 1 cm3

skin sample (Palsbøll, Larsen and Sigurd Hansen 1991) and subsampled for analysis. All samples were placed in 10 mL of 0.2 μm filter-sterilized natural seawater, transported on ice back to the laboratory for culturing within 5 h of collection, and processed immediately. In July 2016, a 14-year-old beluga whale, Delphinapterus leucas, under professional care at the Mystic Aquarium in Mystic, Connecticut was sampled at five sites (right-side front, right-side back, ventral chest, left-side back and left-side peak) with sterile cotton swabs during a routine blood draw procedure. Freshly collected skin swabs were placed in 10 mL of 0.2 μm filter-sterilized natural seawater, transported on ice back to the laboratory within 6 h of collection and processed immediately. Coral tissue + mucus, collected via surface swabs, and mucus samples, collected via syringe, were sampled underwater using SCUBA at 2–3 m from three species of coral, Porites astreoides, Acropora palmata and Millepora alcicornis (two individuals, one individual and one individual, respectively) in St. John, U.S.V.I. (18.31◦N, −64.76◦W). Mucus was collected by gentle syringe pulls (which may have dislodged some coral tissue), and mucus + tissue samples were obtained by swabbing the coral surface using a sterile cotton swab. For all colonies, approximately the same surface area of coral was sampled. Upon surfacing, the syringe samples were held upside down to gravity-concentrate the mucus. Then, the mucus was released from the syringe into the cryovial. The swabs were directly placed in 4% glycerol and frozen in liquid nitrogen vapors and then held at −80◦C until use in culturing experiments. Although it is difficult to distinguish coralassociated bacteria from potentially water-borne bacteria using this sampling method, water immediately surrounding tropical coral contains more coral-associated bacteria, as well as surfaceassociated genes, than water more distantly related to the reefs (1 m off the reef), suggesting a coral association even for potentially water-borne microbes (Weber et al. 2019). Sample details are provided in Table S1 (Supporting Information).

Phylogenetic analysis of bacterial SSU rRNA gene sequences

Taxonomic identifications of each bacterial sequence to the genus level were conducted in ARB (Ludwig 2004). First, the sequences were aligned using SINA web aligner v.1.2.11. This alignment was then imported into ARB software, and sequences were aligned to the SILVA (Pruesse et al. 2007) non-redundant database using default parameters to identify taxonomy to the genus level and in some cases to the species level. The taxonomic identity of the fungal sequences was determined through the ISHAM ITS database (Irinyi et al. 2015). Of the 592 sequenced isolates (i.e. 587 bacterial and five fungal), another 46 sequences with poor quality (i.e. lengths shorter than 600 nucleotides) were removed from the dataset before downstream phylogenetic analysis and tree generation. Of these 46 sequences that were removed, ARB analysis indicated that none represented genera that were not already present among the remaining 546 sequences used to construct the final phylogenetic tree. The remaining sequences >600 bp in length were aligned using MUSCLE alignment in Mega7 using -400 gap open and UPGMB clustering parameters (Edgar 2004). This alignment was used to construct a maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree with 402 informative nucleotide positions in the final dataset. Confidence intervals of the phylogenetic relationships were determined using 1000 bootstrap samples. To minimize sequence redundancy and to enable comparison of taxonomic identity vs. sampled surface and taxonomic identity vs. media type, a second tree was generated by first selecting a single representative sequence from a node of sequences sharing ≥99% similarity, and then realigning these 109 representative sequences in Mega7 as described above. The resulting alignment was used to construct a maximum likelihood tree with 417 informative nucleotide positions in the final data set (Fig. 1). Confidence intervals of the phylogenetic relationships were determined using 1000 bootstrap samples. Both trees were edited in FigTree version 1.4.3 and Adobe Illustrator CS6.

GreenGenes OTU Assignment in QIIME

OTUs were assigned for bacterial isolates. A total of 587 sequences passed a preliminary check for quality for the downstream analyses. OTU assignment was performed using Quantitative Insights Into Microbial Ecology (QIIME, version 1) software running on an Ubuntu virtual machine with default parameters using two algorithms (UCLUST or BLAST) to assign our sequences to fully sequenced microbial genomes sharing 99% similarity to the 16S rRNA gene (GreenGenes 13.5 reference database; Caporaso et al. 2010). The operational taxonomic unit formation was first performed using the QIIME closed reference picking command with default parameters, which uses UCLUST taxon assignment method (Edgar 2004), version 1.2.22q to perform the assignment. The UCLUST algorithm was not successful in assigning 12.9% (75 of 587 sequences) of the sequences; therefore, the OTU assignment of the remaining sequences was performed in QIIME using the BLAST assignment method at 99% similarity to the GreenGenes (13.5 reference database). The OTUs assigned using BLAST were manually added to the OTU table constructed through closed reference picking. Both algorithms together were successful in assigning all sequences to OTUs in the GreenGenes database (Table S4, Supporting Information). Sample diversity was demonstrated through OTU richness by sample type (Smith and Wilson 1996; Table 1).

Multivariate analyses of cultured microbial community composition

Multivariate statistical approaches were used to examine cultured microbial community variation among sample types and media variations. All data manipulation and analysis were conducted in R version 3.6.3 using the packages ‘vegan’ (Oksanen 2018) and ‘Biostats’ (McGarigal 2009). The multivariate analysis compared 102 objects, representing the microbial community composition from every media variation and surface sample (17 whale skin swab samples, eight coral syringe samples, eight coral swab samples) combination. Microorganisms cultured using KJ (fungi-selecting) and AC (Actinobacteria-selecting) media were removed from the analysis because their low microbial culture yield and low OTU richness would skew comparisons of group differences, therefore reducing the analysis to 97 objects. Microbial community composition was analyzed using the presence and absence of 21 microbial families to avoid the disproportionate influence of microbes exhibiting rapid growth on culture media. Similarity between objects was computed using a Jaccard coefficient, an asymmetrical binary coefficient that treats double-zeros in a differently than the other data (Baroni-Urbani and Buser 1976). This asymmetry is important in a culture-dependent experimental context, since a microbe’s observed absence does not necessarily denote a true absence in the sample. A non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) ordination approach was used to visualize microbial community variation among samples and media variations. NMDS attempts to locate objects in a low-dimensional ordination space such that the inter-object distances have the same rank order as the interobject dissimilarities in the original dissimilarity matrix (Digby and Kempton 1987). The NMDS ordination approach was chosen because of its flexibility in choice of similarity coefficient and because it avoids the assumption of linear relationships among variables by using ranked distances. ## RESULTS

Characterization of the cultured bacterial communities

The intense cultivation effort used in this study yielded a phylogenetically diverse array of cultured microbial isolates. A total of 779 pure microbial strains were isolated from the surface microbiomes from 25 animal surface samples representing three coral and two cetacean species (Table S1, Supporting Information). The SSU rRNA gene or ITS1 region was successfully sequenced for 587 bacterial isolates and 5 fungal isolates, respectively, allowing for taxonomic identification of 592 microbial isolates in total. Table S2 (Supporting Information) reports the bacterial and fungal taxonomic identification, Genbank Accession number, and culturing condition that led to their isolation. The remaining unsequenced 187 isolates endure in the culture collection for further genetic and functional exploration. The sequenced culture collection yielded five microbial phyla: Proteobacteria (78.5% of all isolates), Firmicutes (15.9%), Bacteroidetes (3.62%), Actinobacteria (0.987%) and Ascomycota (0.987%; Fig. 1 and Table S3, Supporting Information). Alignment of these sequences within the SILVA 106 database in ARB (Ludwig 2004; Quast et al. 2012) revealed 50 bacterial genera contained within

15 bacterial orders, and alignment with the ISHAM ITS database (Irinyi et al. 2015) revealed two fungal genera found within two additional orders represented in the culturable surface microbiomes of two whale species and three coral species. Most prevalent in coral samples were the presence of members of the Flavobacteriales, Bacillales, Rhodobacterales and Sphingomonadales microbial orders (Fig. 2). In the whale samples, Alteromonadales were the most prominent (Fig. 2). Of the 50 bacterial genera identified in this study, 36% are unique to a single animal surface. However, commonalities exist between sampled species, including genera Sulfitobacter, Alteromonas, Marinobacter and Neptuniibacter, which were found to occur in between 60 and 80% of all samples examined (Fig. 3). Microorganisms associated with the skin of D. leucas were observed to record the lowest OTU richness (Fig. 2). Cultured isolates associated with the coral syringe sampling method were more diverse and had higher OTU richness than cultured isolates associated with coral surface swab isolates. This diversity and richness are found both within and across the three coral species (Table 1). Firmicutes dominated the syringe samples while surface swabs hosted more bacteria in the Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria phyla. Of the 109 OTUs isolated in this study, 54.1% were isolated from the MA media variation only (Fig. 3C). Additionally, the culture media selected for potentially phylogenetically distinct microorganisms, even within the same genus. For example, Gramella sp. 5 and Gramella sp. 6 were both isolated from P. astreoides, but the use of ‘LYS’ and ‘HSL-AMP’ media variations selected for strains with distinct SSU rRNA sequences (Fig. 3C). Bacillus sp. 4 and Bacillus sp. 5 were both isolated from A. palmata, but the use of ‘MA’ and ‘LYS’ media selected for strains with distinct SSU rRNA sequences (Fig. 3C), suggesting closely related isolates could be responding to unique attributes of the culture media. MA media type consistently supported the growth of diverse isolates (Fig. 3). For example, many isolates within genera Paracoccus and Paenibacillus were isolated from MA alone. Phylogenetic analyses of host-microorganism associations

For numerous bacterial genera where multiple OTUs are present, OTUs with divergent SSU rRNA sequences were isolated from distinct animal hosts (Fig. 3B). For example, 14 isolates can be binned into one of six unique OTUs within the genus Gramella. A total of two OTUs within this genus were isolated exclusively from either A. palmata or M. alcicornis from HSL-AMP and MA media types, respectively. A total of 12 genera were cultivated distinctly from a single surface/sample type. For example, the genus Citreicella was isolated only from A. palmata. ## DISCUSSION

This study uses an intensive culturing effort to isolate 592 microbes comprising 50 bacterial genera within 15 orders, from the surface microbiomes of two species of whales and three species of corals, demonstrating the effectiveness of using our methodology and suite of culture conditions in capturing microbial diversity from diverse marine animals (Table S2, Supporting Information). A wealth of knowledge can be gained by using bacterial strains in manipulative experiments to understand disease origin; community dynamics relating to resistance, resilience and persistence; functional roles of microbiome members; and impacts on host health. However, investigations have been severely limited by the availability of phylogenetically diverse microbes in culture as efforts to recover and isolate marine microbes from environmental samples struggle to overcome microbial culturing challenges (Dance 2020). This study is also the first to develop a comprehensive collection of cultured bacteria associated with the skin of healthy cetaceans, supplementing the growing body of literature examining the culturable bacteria of cetacean respiratory and digestive systems (Buck et al. 2006; Venn-Watson, Smith and Jensen 2008; Morris et al. 2011; Godoy-Vitorino et al. 2017). Additionally, efforts outlined here yielded a cultured microbial collection, from coral tissue and mucus, greater in phylogenetic diversity and total number of strains recovered than catalogued previously (Lampert et al. 2006; Chimetto et al. 2008; Shnit-Orland and Kushmaro 2009; Galkiewicz et al. 2011). Moreover, 36% of the isolates were unique to a single animal surface, indicating our culturing technique is capable of capturing highly diverse bacterial isolates from diverse host organisms. Strain specificity is a common feature in many symbiotic relationships, and strain-level genetic differences can exist in symbionts, particularly for bacteria (Bongrand and Ruby 2019; Apprill 2020). Culture-independent analyses of coralassociated bacteria find sub-genus phylogenetic clusters represented exclusively in one clade of Scleractinian coral, including strains within the genus Ruegeria, isolated in this study (Huggett and Apprill 2018). The potential for strain specificity to host origin is found in many instances in this study, since OTUs grouped by 99% similarity within the same bacterial genus were isolated solely from separate hosts (Fig. 3). These potential host-specific strains include bacteria within the genera Ruegeria, Paracoccus, Maricaulis, Pseudomonas, Pseudoalteromonas, Idiomarina and Gramella. A total of four of these genera—Ruegeria, Paracoccus, Idiomarina and Gramella—may contain distinct bacterial strains isolated exclusively from different coral species in the same environment. Further examination is needed to indicate if these associations are host-driven rather than environment-driven, and understanding the factors driving host-specific strain association requires interrogation of the host microscale environmental and bacterial species-specific metabolic characteristics and exchange to more fully resolve stable host-bacterial relationships (Ziemert et al. 2014; M¨onnich et al. 2020). Acquisition of bacteria detected in previous culture-independent efforts

Cetacean skin microbes isolated here resemble the main phyla identified through culture-independent methods from Tursiops sp. blow (Bik et al. 2016; Nelson et al. 2019), skin microbiota from Tursiops truncatus and Orcinus orca (Chiarello et al. 2017) and the oral microbiome of Delphinus delphis, Stenella coeruleoalba and Phocoena phocoena (Soares-Castro et al. 2019) which are also dominated by Proteobacteria, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes. Additionally, at the family level, our study was successful in isolating representatives from the Roseobacter clade, one of the most dominant groups of surface colonizers previously identified from the

skin of killer whales (Chiarello et al. 2017). However, isolates that we obtained from humpback whale skin through cultivation are phylogenetically distinct from core members of the skin of this same species as identified through previous cultivationindependent surveys. Although phylogenetic analyses of humpback whale microbiomes reveal the ubiquitous and abundant presence of Tenacibaculum sp. and Psychrobacter sp. across humpback whale populations, other less-abundant microbial genera exhibit temporal shifts in presence and absence, throughout the foraging season and between whales inhabiting different geographic regions (Apprill et al. 2014; Bierlich et al. 2017). Of these less abundant genera, we did have success in cultivating 14 of the 43 (approx. 32.5%) differentially present bacterial genera found to be distinct from the core microbial members (14 of 49 (29%) of all bacterial genera identified); (Bierlich et al. 2017). Understanding these temporally and geographically variable bacterial–host associations can provide insight into the ecological roles of the microorganisms and the biochemical and environmental drivers of microbial community shifts.

We were also able to culture 268 bacterial isolates from coral surface swabs and syringe samples (115 and 153 isolates, respectively). Of these isolates, the most frequently recovered species from coral swab and syringe samples were members in the orders Flavobacteriales, Bacillales, Rhodobacterales, Alteromonadales and Sphingomonadales (Fig. 2). Each of these bacterial orders have been previously identified in surveys of 16S rRNA genes from the microbiomes of Caribbean corals (Sunagawa, Woodley and Medina 2010; Morrow et al. 2012; Kimes et al. 2013; Ainsworth et al. 2015; Apprill, Weber and Santoro 2016). Furthermore, representatives of the family Rhodobacteraceae and the genera Bacillus, Erythrobacter, Gramella, Marinobacter, Neptuniibacter and Oceanobacillus were recovered from all three coral species studied, and each of these genera have been documented on P. astreoides and A. palmata (Fig. 3 and Table S2, Supporting Information; Sharp, Distel and Paul 2012; McDevitt-Irwin et al. 2017). Roseobacter clade-associated bacteria, members of the family Rhodobacteraceae, and the genus Marinobacter are known to associate with P. astreoides throughout the coral life cycle, and these bacteria may be passed down from coral parent to larvae (Sharp, Distel and Paul 2012), which could be a mechanism to retain select metabolically distinct bacterial strains. Marine Roseobacter strains are known to facilitate coral settlement (Sharp et al. 2015). Additionally, we were able to isolate representatives from Halomonas, Hyphomonas, Microbulbifer, Paenibacillus, Photobacterium, Pseudovibrio and Oceanicola (Table S2, Supporting Information) frequently found on both healthy and diseased P. astreoides colonies (McKew et al. 2012; Meyer, Paul and Teplitski 2014; Staley et al. 2017).

Multivariate analyses highlight variation in cultured microbial communities

The non-metric multidimensional (NMDS) ordination and per- MANOVA tests of group differences indicated that cultured microbial community composition differs across sampled species rather than across culture condition (Fig. 4A). However, the global group difference across sampled species is largely driven by the difference between M. novaeangliae and the three

coral species. Significant differences between coral species are likely driven by differences in multivariate dispersion, since cultured microbial communities from A. palmata samples were relatively similar and less disperse between samples. This result suggests that variation in cultured microbial community composition is associated with differences in environment and biological characteristics of the species surface, rather than culture media composition, like nutrient availability or the presence of quorum sensing molecules, for example. Despite their use for targeted cultivation, media variations did not select for particular bacterial clades (Fig. 4A). Additionally, the AC media, designed to select for microorganisms within the Actinobacteria phylum, did not select for any bacteria within this phylum and instead allowed for the growth of three OTUs within the order Bacillales. The Bacillales order contains many sporeproducing organisms. It is possible that the heat shock may have selected for heat-resistant spores that structurally, metabolically and functionally differ from vegetative cells (Gopal et al. 2015). Due to time constraints, microbial biomass from D. leucas samples were cryopreserved before colony picking, likely selecting for microbes with rapid growth. The bias induced by the microbial isolation method for the D. leucas samples produced low microbial OTU richness and resulted in a less robust dataset that inhibited model convergence in multivariate analyses. This bias underscores the importance of immediate microbial isolation upon surface sampling. The NMDS ordination and perMANOVA test of group differences indicated that cultured microbial community composition differs between coral sampling method, with swab samples enriched with microbes in the Oceanospirillaceae, Rhodobaccteraceae and Alteromonadaceae families and syringe samples enriched with microbes from Bacillaceae and Staphylococcaceae families (Fig. 5). The syringe sampling method more likely recovers microorganisms contained in the coral mucus, while the swabbing method more likely recovers microorganisms attached to the coral surface. Culture-dependent design introduces bias in recovered microorganisms

Many of the culturable bacteria from both whale and coral species included Alteromonas sp. (Fig. 2), which are globally distributed marine copiotrophic bacteria that dominate in heterotrophic blooms and outcompete other bacteria due to their rapid growth when organic nutrients are readily available (Math et al. 2012). The ubiquity of this genus in our whale samples could have resulted due to the nutrient-rich media base used during cultivation, which has previously led to an overestimation of their abundance in the environment due to the ease at which the cells form colonies on agar plates and the voracity with which they take advantage of sporadic inputs of organic matter (Behringer et al. 2018). However, our data indicate that a fraction of the 127 Alteromonas strains isolated here were only found on coral or on cetaceans, indicating potential host specificity for particular strains. Additionally, isolates that are phylogenetically similar can exhibit different biochemical profiles and functional roles (Lampert et al. 2006). Culture independent studies by themselves would likely fail to link varied contributions of similar strains to larger implications, such as their effects on host fitness. Future studies should integrate more diverse media types, particularly low nutrient conditions, to target more slower growing microorganisms that might have been overlooked in this study.

## CONCLUSION

The dermis represents both a first line of defense for marine animals, and an environment uniquely colonized by phylogenetically and functionally diverse bacterial representatives. The challenge for marine microbial ecology remains in linking the phylogenetic diversity of host-associated microbes to their functional roles within the community. Progress will depend on merging data from sequencing-based studies with manipulative experiments using cultured isolates, thereby providing insight on nutrient cycling capacity, interspecies communication, defense against pathogens and parasites, host immune response, wound repair, microbial community succession and benefits to host development, health and survival (Krediet et al. 2013; Meyer, Paul and Teplitski 2014; Medina et al. 2017; Bell, Garland and Alford 2018; Longford et al. 2019; van Oppen and Blackall 2019). Moreover, culture-based methods have already proven successful in conservation efforts in terrestrial ecosystems (Daskin et al. 2014; Loudon et al. 2014) and could prove

equally as valuable in marine systems (van Oppen and Blackall 2019). Our culturable library holds great promise for future manipulative experiments that can examine the metabolic factors and surface properties influencing complementary associations between animal host and microbe, as our study was able to capture a rich repository of marine microbes and inspires new questions that will undoubtedly fuel future research into the varied and elusive roles of marine microbes.

# Temporal reorganization of maternal care during early life stress in mice

**Authors:** Hannah Jo; Eman Ali; Catherine Jensen Peña

**Affiliations:** 1Princeton Neuroscience Institute, Princeton University, 40 Woodlands Way, Princeton, NJ, 08544, USA

## Abstract

Maternal separation is a widely used early-life stress (ELS) paradigm in rodents. Disrupted maternal care by separation of pups from the dam for several hours per day across neonatal and juvenile development has been found to alter hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function, molecular and circuit-level brain development and function, and behaviors associated with anxiety, depression, and cognition. However, dams have been found to temporarily increase their care towards pups upon reunion — typically associated with positive outcome measures — calling into question whether this increase in care compensates for care lost during separation. Using a mouse model of ELS, we quantified maternal home cage behaviors from postnatal day P2-16 across three observation periods per day (prior to maternal separation, immediately following reunion, and several hours following reunion), with maternal separation beginning on P10. Four composite variables of home cage behavior frequency were created: total dam-pup contact, rough contact, no contact, and dam self-care. Consistent with previous reports, we found a transient increase in care upon reunion, along with an increase in rough contact and a decrease in dam self-care. We then calculated geometric area-under-curve across the day and found that the increase in total contact among ELS litters does not result in overall more care, as indicated in previous publications, but rather a temporal reorganization of care. These findings provide important nuance to understand how maternal separation disrupts offspring care.

Keywords: Maternal separation, Early-life stress, Early life adversity, Maternal behavior

## Introduction

The extent and type of care that offspring receive in early life can affect mental and physical health across the lifespan. In humans, adverse childhood experiences are associated with increased risk for mental health syndromes including depression, anxiety, and addiction, and physical health challenges including cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease, and even immune disorders and cancer (Felitti et al., 1998; Gilbert et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2017). Rodent models of early-life stress (ELS) have been a useful tool for understanding the consequences of the early environment on offspring wellbeing and neurodevelopment. Maternal separation is a widely used ELS paradigm which involves separating pups from their dams for several hours per day (Plotsky and Meaney, 1993; Tractenberg et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024; Pryce et al., 2005). This separation is thought to model aspects of deprivation (Murthy and Gould, 2018). Maternal separation paradigms vary across research groups as to timing or age of separation, whether pups or dams are separated from the home cage, and whether siblings are kept together during separation or housed individually (Tractenberg et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024). Maternal separation has been found to increase corticosterone response to stressors, altering hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA)-axis regulation, emotional dysregulation, and anxiety-and-depression-like behaviors (Anisman et al., 1998; Fóscolo et al., 2022; Lippmann et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2000; Pihoker et al., 1993; Plotsky and Meaney, 1993; Vargas et al., 2016).

Interestingly, when separated pups are reunited with their mothers after both short or long periods of separation, dams have been observed to increase their care towards pups (de Sá Couto-Pereira et al., 2016; Granata et al., 2022; Macri et al., 2004; Millstein and Holmes, 2007; Pryce et al., 2001; Stamatakis et al., 2015; Zimmerberg et al., 2003; Baracz et al., 2020; Macrì et al., 2008). Dams, or indeed other caring alloparents, will naturally retrieve scattered pups to a nest (Beach and Jaynes, 1956; Fleming and Rosenblatt, 1974; Reisbick et al., 1975) and begin licking and grooming pups (Champagne et al., 2003; Stern and Johnson, 1989), which is associated with positive stress regulation and other positive developmental effects (Liu et al., 1997; Meaney, 2001; Weaver et al., 2004). Together, these observations have begged the question of whether maternal separation paradigms prompt an increase in care that compensates for the stress of separation (Orso et al., 2019). While many long-term negative consequences of maternal separation have been documented, these observations nevertheless call into question the effects of the paradigm. A few studies have made multiple observations across the day to determine how long increases in post-reunion care persist (de Sá Couto-Pereira et al., 2016; Granata et al., 2022; Macrì et al., 2008), though none have explicitly calculated effects relative to loss of care during separation. It is therefore not currently known whether these increases in care may actually make up for the care missed during the period of separation.

To help reconcile the literature, we sought to determine whether maternal separation increases maternal care transiently or throughout the day in C57BL/6 mice. We hypothesized that increased care following dam-pup reunion may be transient and insufficient to compensate for the lack of care experienced during the hours of separation. To test this, we observed home cage behaviors at three time points throughout the day from postnatal days P2-17. We used an ELS paradigm in which pups are separated from their dams for three-four hours per day during a late juvenile period from postnatal days P10-17, allowing us to observe how ELS alters maternal behavior both within and across groups (Peña et al., 2017). By including multiple periods of observation before the start of maternal separation, immediately following pup reunion, and several hours after reunion, we sought to provide a more nuanced profile of how maternal separation disrupts total contact and dynamic timing of maternal care.

## Methods

### Animals

C57BL/6J mice were maintained on a 12-h light/dark cycle (lights on at 4 a.m.) with ad libitum access to food and water. All experiments were conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Princeton University. All behavioral testing occurred during the animals’ light cycle. Mating occurred in-house to prevent shipping stress during gestation. Two multiparous adult (6-8 months) C57BL/6J female mice were mated with one male. Males were removed after 5 days and females were separated into individual maternity cages 1–3 days prior to parturition. Litters were weighed and counted and cages cleaned on the day of birth (PND0) and minimally balanced when necessary and possible to have between 4 and 9 pups (average litter size 6.26 pups; average male/female ratio 0.8) but were otherwise left undisturbed. Litter size and ratio did not differ by group. Cages were cleaned with minimal disruption to the litter once/week. Standard-reared cages included EnviroDri nesting material and a cardboard hut as enrichment. Offspring were weaned at postnatal PND21.

### Early life stress

All litters were randomly assigned to standard-rearing (n = 7) or ELS (n = 9) conditions. ELS was administered from postnatal day P10 to 17 as previously described (Balouek et al., 2023; Parel et al., 2023; Peña et al., 2017) and consisted of a combination of maternal separation for 3-4 h per day during the light cycle and limiting home cage resources. Enrichment huts were removed from ELS cages and nesting material was depleted to ½ of an EnviroDri nesting puck during the week of ELS. On each separation day, the entire litter of pups was removed to a clean cage with clean bedding material and returned to the home cage at the end of the separation period. Start times were varied 1-3 h across days to prevent habituation. Pups were given access to hydrogel in the separation cages, but none were observed to eat it. Nesting material was restored at the end of ELS. The impact of ELS on offspring from these litters was reported previously (Parel et al., 2023).

### Observations of home cage dam behaviors

Home cage maternal behavior was scored as previously described (Champagne et al., 2003; Jensen Peña and Champagne, 2013; Peña et al., 2013). Maternal behavior was observed for three 60-min observation periods daily during P1-16 (Fig. 1A), such that all cages were observed before the start of ELS (P1-9) and for the first week of ELS (P10-16). Observations ended one day prior to the completion of ELS for unplanned reasons. Every day, three 60-min observations were conducted per cage: the first observation was 1 h prior to pup separation, the second was immediately post-reunion (i.e. the first hour following dam-pup reunion), and the third observation was later post-reunion (i.e. 2-3 h after reunion) (Fig. 1A). The time of maternal separation was purposefully varied each day to prevent habituation, and thus four post-reunion observations were done in the dark cycle under red light. Behavioral observations were made every 3 min during each observation period for a total of 20 observations per hour (Champagne et al., 2003). The frequency of each behavior was calculated as the number of observations of the behavior divided by the total number of observations, and then transformed as percent time. The following individual behaviors were scored: nursing, licking/grooming, licking/grooming and nursing (LGN), passive contact, “hut” (when dams and pups were together in an enrichment hut), pup retrieval, pup stepping, nest building, dam eating, dam drinking, dam self-grooming, and no-contact/other. Notably, standard-reared “Std” cages had enrichment huts preventing observation of individual behaviors beyond dam-pup contact. Thus, “hut” time is considered as contact with pups but prevents distinguishing between passive contact, licking/grooming, and nursing that was more readily observable in ELS cages without the hut. We then created three composite behaviors: total contact (i.e. time in hut, time in observed contact, licking/grooming, LGN, and nursing), rough contact (i.e. pup stepping, pup retrieval, and nest building during which pups are often disrupted and stepped on but that isn't the primary behavior of the dam), and dam self-care (i.e. dam eating, drinking, and self-grooming) (Fig. 1B).

Home-cage behavior was scored in three 1h sessions: 1 h before separation, 1 h after separation, and 2-3 h after reunion. B) Composite frequency scores were created for active contact, rough contact, and self-care behaviors.*

### Statistics

Statistical analyses were performed in R (Version 4.5) and GraphPad Prism (Version 10). Pairwise group comparisons were performed using an unpaired two-tailed student's t-test. Analysis of maternal behavior over time (days and hours) was conducted with repeated measures ANOVA, followed by Tukey's HSD post hoc tests when appropriate. Differences in proportion between groups were calculated using a chi-squared test for non-parametrical categorical data, with post hoc pairwise comparisons based on adjusted p-values. Total contact with pups was calculated as geometric area under curve (AUC) for each “bin” of time: during the 3 h period of separation (Bin 1), during the 3 h following reunion (Bin 2), and for the remainder of the day (Bin 3; 18 h). Calculations were made using average contact frequency after P10, by litter. Significance was set at the p < 0.05 level.

## Results

Dams engage in a variety of pup-directed and self-directed home cage behaviors, the frequency of which changes across the postpartum period and circadian cycle (Champagne et al., 2003; Jensen Peña and Champagne, 2013). We first quantified twelve home cage behaviors and examined how the overall frequency distribution of mouse dam behaviors differed as a function of developmental phase and group. Proportion of time spent in each individual behavior was aggregated by dam across either P1-9 or 10-16, and then averaged by group (Fig. 2). Consistent with observations of maternal behavior in rats (Champagne et al., 2003), total time in contact with pups (licking, nursing, LGN, other contact, or hut-obscured pup contact) decreased somewhat from the early (P1-9) to later (P10-16) postpartum period among Std dams [mean 78.6 ± 6.7% to 62.1 ± 15.1% of time; paired t-test: t(1,6) = 2.95, p = 0.026]. This change was largely attributable to increases in eating and time not in contact with pups (Fig. 2). Decreased contact was mitigated somewhat among ELS-assigned dams (mean 74.1 ± 8.3%; t(1,8) = 1.86, p = 0.100). A chi-squared test for non-parametrical categorical data revealed that the distribution of behaviors differed significantly (χ2(24) = 194.88, p < 0.05). Post-hoc tests of the chi-square indicate that differences in dam self-care accounted for the largest share of the overall effect, suggesting that ELS dams allocated time away from pup-directed care and toward self-directed behaviors.

Note, enrichment huts given to STD cages were removed during ELS enabling more detailed observations. “Hut” is therefore considered dam-pup contact but individual behaviors were obscured.*

Next, we focused on the effect of ELS after P10. We generated composite variables for total contact time, rough contact, and self-care behavior, as described in methods. We first calculated the mean frequency of each composite behavior across all observations, regardless of postpartum day or time of day (Fig. 3A–D). ELS moderately increased total contact time [Fig. 3A; unpaired two-tailed t-test: t(1,8) = 1.885, p = 0.093] and rough contact with pups [Fig. 3C; t(1,8) = 2.951, p = 0.011], and decreased time not in contact with pups [Fig. 3B; t(1,8) = 2.81, p = 0.0140]. Total self-care was not substantially altered by ELS [Fig. 3D; t(1,8) = 1.67, p = 0.117]. These behavioral shifts among ELS dams were present across ELS days, and not limited to only the first days of the manipulation, for example (Supplemental Fig. 1).

Boxes show median and whiskers extending to 1.5×IQR; jittered points represent individual litters.*

We next sought to determine whether ELS altered home cage behaviors across the day, or whether changes in behavior were specific to the period following reunion. To do this, we restricted analyses to the post-P10 period to characterize how these group differences unfolded across the reunion window. For each dam, we aggregated total observed contact at - 1h (morning baseline), +1 h (immediately post-reunion), and +2-3h (late window). A two-way repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of time, F(1.55, 21.63) = 22.14, p < 0.001, with a significant group × time interaction [Fig. 4A; F(1.55, 21.63) = 8.55, p = 0.0034]. The main effect of the group showed a trend toward higher overall observed contact in ELS dams, [F(1,14) = 4.20, p = 0.0597]. Post-hoc comparisons using estimated marginal means with Tukey adjustment showed that ELS dams exhibited higher observed contact than Std dams at the +1h timepoint (ELS - Std = 6.233, Tukey-adjusted p = 0.0046), whereas groups did not differ at -1h or +2-3h timepoints.

Ribbons reflect standard-error; points represent individual litters.*

No-contact behavior also varied by condition and time with significant main effects of group, [Fig. 4B; F(1,14) = 7.09, p = 0.0185, and time, F(1.59, 22.21) = 6.23, p = 0.0107]. In addition, there was a significant group × time interaction F(1.59, 22.21) = 5.54, p = 0.0159. Std dams exhibited more no-contact behavior than ELS dams at +1 h and +2-3h, but not at an hour prior to reunion. Rough contact showed a significant main effect of the group [Fig. 4C; F(1,14) = 7.88, p = 0.0140], with ELS dams exhibiting higher rough contact overall. However, there was no significant effect of time, F(1.90, 26.54) = 0.28, p = 0.747, and no group × time interaction, F(1.90, 26.54) = 2.19, p = 0.134. Thus, this increase is notably stable across the reunion window. Self-care varied across the reunion window (Fig. 4D), showing a significant effect of time, F(1.50, 20.99) = 24.84, p < 0.001, and a significant Group × Time interaction, F(1.50, 20.99) = 5.72, p = 0.0161, but no main effect of group, F(1,14) = 2.78, p = 0.117. Post-hoc comparisons show that Std dams showed higher self-care than ELS dams at the +1h timepoint (Std - ELS - 3.680, Tukey-adjusted p = 0.0095), whereas groups did not differ at -1h or +2-3h. Together, we found that ELS alters the temporal organization of maternal behavior after reunion, with ELS dams showing increased immediate post-reunion contact, reduced no-contact, elevated rough contact, and relatively decreased self-care.

To account for the fact that half of the third (+2-3h) observations were done in the dark phase, given the purposely varied time of maternal separation each day, we determined whether ELS impacted behavior across the phase transition. It is known that pup grooming, nursing, and contact are elevated in the light compared to dark phase, and self-care behaviors are elevated in the dark compared to light phases (Jensen Peña and Champagne, 2013). Our data replicates this, with a main effect of dark to decrease total contact [Supplemental Fig. 2; F(1,14) = 44.20, p < 0.0001] and increase self-care [F(1,14) = 47.14, p < 0.0001]. There was also an interaction between phase and ELS for both behaviors, such that ELS seems to blunt the effect of phase on behavior [total contact: F(1,14) = 6.578, p = 0.023; self-care: F(1,14) = 10.12, p = 0.007], consistent with an interpretation that ELS alters the temporal organization of care.

Finally, we asked whether the increase in post-reunion contact in ELS dams is sufficient to compensate for the contact that is necessarily lost during separation. We first plotted total group-mean contact among Std litters across the 3-h separation interval, 3-h immediate post-reunion period, and remainder of the day (Fig. 5A: Bins 1, 2, and 3, respectively), assuming linear rise in contact between the post-reunion and next pre-reunion measurement periods. We then calculated area-under-curve for each time bin, by litter. While there is an increase in care in the 3-h bin following reunion of ELS pups, this increase was insufficient to make up for the care lost during the 3 h of separation such that total contact across Bins 1 and 2 was still lower among ELS mice (Fig. 5B; Welch's two-tailed t-test for unequal distributions: t(1,8) = 3.729, p = 0.008). Total contact across the day was not significantly different between groups (Fig. 5B). These findings indicate that maternal separation induces temporal reorganization of care, rather than overall more or less care.
